title: Gerundio: Bolívar y San Martín en paralelo

sections.content: When two campaigns run at once, the gerund lets a sentence pack in what someone was doing alongside the main action — organizing an army before crossing, descending unexpectedly, resigning surprisingly. These sentences are taken directly from the previous reading.

items.spanish: San Martín se movía desde el sur, organizando un ejército en Argentina antes de cruzar los Andes.
items.english: San Martín moved from the south, organizing an army in Argentina before crossing the Andes.

items.spanish: Ambas campañas, actuando de manera independiente pero con un objetivo compartido, convergerían finalmente en Perú.
items.english: Both campaigns, acting independently but with a shared goal, would finally converge in Peru.

items.spanish: Descendiendo inesperadamente sobre territorio neogranadino, sus fuerzas lograron una victoria decisiva en Boyacá.
items.english: Descending unexpectedly onto New Granadan territory, his forces achieved a decisive victory at Boyacá.

items.spanish: San Martín, renunciando sorprendentemente a su cargo, se retiró por completo de la vida pública.
items.english: San Martín, surprisingly resigning his post, withdrew completely from public life.

sections.content: Notice how the gerund can sit right next to the subject with commas on both sides (San Martín, renunciando..., se retiró) — this reads almost like an aside, adding a second fact about the subject without making it the main point of the sentence.
